title: Vayera: Abimelech (Genesis 20)
hook: a foreign king turns out more upright than Abraham feared

segments.voice: Yesterday in Vayera, Abraham argued for a city of strangers: shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly? Your line was justice, even from God.

You move to a new town, or start a new job, or travel somewhere far away. Before you've met anyone, you've already decided a few things. People here are cold. People here can't be trusted. Better keep your guard up. Sometimes that instinct protects you. And sometimes it's just wrong, and the people you braced against turn out to be decent. Abraham, the great hero of this portion, the one who just argued for strangers, walks into a foreign town with exactly that fear.
screen: `BEFORE YOU'VE MET ANYONE.` → `KEEP YOUR GUARD UP.` → `ABRAHAM WALKS INTO GERAR.`

segments.voice: Abraham and Sarah travel to Gerar, ruled by a king named Abimelech. Abraham tells people Sarah is his sister, not his wife. So Abimelech, thinking she's unmarried, takes her into his house. That night God comes to Abimelech in a dream and warns him: she's a married woman. Abimelech, who hasn't touched her, protests. He asks God, in effect, will you destroy even a righteous nation? He said she was his sister. She said he was her brother. I did this with a clean heart and clean hands. Listen to that question. It echoes Abraham's own from yesterday, shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly, now in the mouth of a foreign king. And God agrees: I know you did this with a clean heart; that's why I kept you from sinning. Return her. The text adds something: Abraham is a prophet, and he'll pray for you. In the morning Abimelech calls Abraham and asks: what did you see, that you did this thing? And Abraham answers: "Surely the fear of God is not in this place." He assumed these people had no conscience. The story shows otherwise. Abimelech returns Sarah, gives sheep and oxen and servants, and says: my land is before you; live wherever you like. Then Abraham prays for Abimelech's household, and they're healed. The story lets the founder of the Jewish people be wrong about strangers, and lets a foreign king be the one with the clean heart.
screen: `SHE IS MY SISTER.` · `A CLEAN HEART AND CLEAN HANDS.` · `NO FEAR OF GOD IN THIS PLACE.` · `ABRAHAM PRAYS, AND THEY'RE HEALED.` · then, large: `GOODNESS IS EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Bring back a time someone you had braced against, a new neighbor, an official at a counter, a coworker, a person on the street, turned out to be kind or fair. Remember what they actually did, then what you had expected instead. Let the gap between the two sit with you for a moment, without judging yourself.
Vayera. The portion where Abraham fears a foreign king, and the king turns out more upright than he feared.
Your line: goodness is everywhere. Even in Gerar, where Abraham had expected none. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jewish commentators read Genesis 20 as a story in which Abraham's fear of strangers proves mistaken, and note that here God calls Abraham a prophet who will pray for the king.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of the Genesis 20:11 clause ('Surely the fear of God is not in this place').
20:4–5 (Abimelech's protest, 'in the simplicity/integrity of my heart and innocency of my hands') is paraphrased as 'a clean heart and clean hands'.
Claims of firsts: navi (20:7) as the Torah's first use of 'prophet', and 20:17 as the first explicit use of the verb 'pray' (hitpallel). Confirm both.
Abraham's partial justification (20:12: Sarah is his half-sister) is omitted; consider whether a Keeper wants it for fairness to Abraham.
The script avoids moral judgment of Abraham beyond his own admitted fear; confirm tone.
